name: Shashmaqam (Tajik-Uzbek classical)
lineage: Bukharan Central Asian classical six-modal-cycle tradition shared between Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. The six modal cycles — Buzruk, Rost, Navo, Dugoh, Segoh, Iroq — each a multi-movement suite structure. Origin in Bukhara city under the Bukharan emirate, present form crystallized in the eighteenth century. Canonical instrumentation: tanbur long-necked plucked lute as the primary maqom voice carrier, dutar two-string fretted lute, sato bowed tanbur, ghijak spike fiddle (analogue to Azerbaijani kamancha), doira frame-drum with internal jingles, nay end-blown reed flute. The Bukharan Jewish community preserved the most archaic transmission layer through Soviet-era suppression and subsequent diaspora-recovery in the United States and Israel. Twentieth-century master Turgun Alimatov (tanbur, dutar, sato virtuoso) anchored the post-Soviet revival. Distinguished from Azerbaijani mugham by six-maqom-cycle structure (vs Azerbaijani seven-dastgah); distinguished from Persian dastgah-i radif by Bukharan ensemble configuration and Tajik-Persian-language sufyiana-poetry textual base; distinguished from Uyghur muqam by Bukharan-Tajik dialect-specific cadential and modal vocabulary
